evidence.claim: US 75 alternates between the Missouri River plain and rolling hills on Nebraska’s Lewis & Clark Scenic Byway.
evidence.quote: Here the two highways run concurrently to the north as they emerge from the rolling hills back into the Missouri River plain as they pass through the village of Homer.

evidence.claim: The Nebraska Department of Transportation lists 82 miles from just north of Omaha to South Sioux City.
evidence.quote: Lewis & Clark Scenic Byway 82 miles from just north of Omaha to South Sioux City along U.S. Highway 75.

evidence.claim: Visit Nebraska highlights cropland, wooded river bluffs and Native American culture along the scenic route.
evidence.quote: Through bountiful cropland and beautifully wooded bluffs framing the Missouri River, you’ll discover Native American culture

evidence.claim: Lewis and Clark traveled up this Missouri corridor in 1804, and several former campsites lie near the highway.
evidence.quote: It was the primary exploration route taken by the Lewis and Clark Expedition as they traveled up the Missouri River in 1804. There are several locations along the US 75 corridor that feature former campsite locations of the expedition.

evidence.claim: The US 75 number arrived on the Nebraska route north of Omaha much later.
evidence.quote: In 1984, with the completion of Interstate 29 in Iowa, a series of transfers between Iowa and Nebraska brought the US 75 designation from the I-29 corridor into Nebraska from Omaha north

evidence.claim: Previously, US 75 crossed into Iowa at Omaha; in 1984, the designation moved west of the river, replacing US 73 north of Dawson.
evidence.quote: suggested removing the US 75 designation from the I-29 corridor in Iowa and assigning it to the former US 73 route north of Dawson in Nebraska.

evidence.claim: Previously, US 75 crossed into Iowa at Omaha
evidence.quote: In Omaha, US 75 turned east to cross the Missouri River into Iowa

evidence.claim: in 1984, the designation moved west of the river
evidence.quote: the transfer was made official on December 5, 1984.

evidence.claim: For a southbound drive, leave South Sioux City toward Homer, then climb from the river plain toward Winnebago and Macy.
evidence.quote: Here the two highways run concurrently to the north as they emerge from the rolling hills back into the Missouri River plain as they pass through the village of Homer.

evidence.claim: Macy is the tribal seat of the Omaha Reservation.
evidence.quote: into the Omaha Reservation towards the tribal seat of Macy.

evidence.claim: At Decatur, descend to the edge of the plain and follow agricultural fields toward Tekamah, Herman and Blair.
evidence.quote: The highway continues north out of Tekamah, still following the edge of the rolling hills and Missouri River plain passing through rich agricultural fields

evidence.claim: Beyond Blair, continue to Fort Calhoun and the rolling hills north of Omaha.
evidence.quote: the highway winds its way through rolling hills before entering the Missouri River plain just south of Fort Calhoun. From here, the highway continues its northward travel along the edge of the river plain towards Blair.

evidence.claim: leave South Sioux City toward Homer
evidence.quote: the highway approaches an interchange with I-129 and US 20 on the southwest side of South Sioux City.

evidence.claim: The Winnebago Tribe’s buffalo herd has a pasture in the village, and its annual Homecoming Powwow takes place on the last full weekend in July.
evidence.quote: The last full weekend in July, head to the Winnebago Indian Reservation for the tribe’s annual Homecoming Powwow. Year 'round, visit the pasture of the tribe’s buffalo herd, also located in Winnebago.

evidence.claim: Winnebago lies within the tribe’s reservation in northeastern Nebraska.
evidence.quote: Winnebago is located within the Winnebago Reservation of the Ho-Chunk, in the northeast part of Nebraska.

evidence.claim: The village is called Nįšoc in the Hoocąk language; Ho-Chunk is the tribe’s name for itself.
evidence.quote: The village is known as Nįšoc in the Hoocąk language.

evidence.claim: Both the village and its first post office, established in 1867, took their names from the tribe.
evidence.quote: The first post office at Winnebago was established in 1867, within the Winnebago Reservation established primarily in Thurston County, Nebraska. Both were named for the federally recognized Winnebago tribe

evidence.claim: Ho-Chunk is the tribe’s name for itself.
evidence.quote: whose name for themselves (autonym) in their own language is transliterated as Ho-Chunk.

evidence.claim: A trading post at the mouth of Wood Creek helped shape Decatur, beside the upper Missouri River.
evidence.quote: Peter Sarpy helped lay out the town, which developed around his Indian trading post at the mouth of Wood Creek.

evidence.claim: Peter Sarpy helped lay out the settlement, which incorporated in 1856 as the Decatur Townsite & Ferry Company.
evidence.quote: The town of Decatur was incorporated in 1856 under the name "The Decatur Townsite & Ferry Company."

evidence.claim: Its name came from incorporator Stephen Decatur, a former schoolteacher who arrived in 1841.
evidence.quote: This town is named after one of its incorporators, Stephen Decatur.

evidence.claim: He called his farm Decatur Springs; its spring supplied the village with water for the next century.
evidence.quote: His farm was called Decatur Springs, after a spring which supplied water to the village for the next century.

evidence.claim: The Omaha had long occupied this country along the creeks and river before the town developed.
evidence.quote: The area was long occupied by the Omaha Native Americans, who settled along the creeks and river

evidence.claim: beside the upper Missouri River
evidence.quote: Decatur is a village in Burt County, Nebraska, United States, adjacent to the upper Missouri River.

evidence.claim: a former schoolteacher who arrived in 1841
evidence.quote: Stephen Decatur arrived in the area in 1841. A former schoolteacher in New Jersey and New York

evidence.claim: The fort at this state historical park is a reconstruction from the 1980s and 1990s.
evidence.quote: A replica fort was constructed by the state at the site during the 1980s–1990s.

evidence.claim: The original post’s beginnings were below the bluff: soldiers arriving in 1819 built Cantonment Missouri on the river bottom.
evidence.quote: The expedition stopped to build Cantonment Missouri, a winter camp along the river bottom below the bluffs.

evidence.claim: After the Missouri flooded that camp in spring 1820, they built a permanent post atop Council Bluff and named it Fort Atkinson.
evidence.quote: In the spring of 1820, the Missouri River flooded Cantonment Missouri.  The soldiers built a permanent camp atop Council Bluff, and renamed it Fort Atkinson.

evidence.claim: Clark had recommended the bluff after the expedition’s 1804 council with members of the Oto and Missouria tribes.
evidence.quote: the site of an August 1804 council between the Lewis and Clark Expedition and members of the Oto and Missouria Native American tribes.

evidence.claim: The Army abandoned the fort in 1827.
evidence.quote: In 1827, the Army abandoned the fort at Council Bluff

evidence.claim: soldiers arriving in 1819
evidence.quote: Fifteen years later, in 1819, President James Monroe dispatched a military expedition

evidence.claim: Clark had recommended the bluff
evidence.quote: William Clark recommended the high bluff overlooking the Missouri River to the United States government as a suitable location to build a fort.

evidence.claim: Near Dakota City, the drive uses a four-lane divided highway; south toward Homer, it narrows to two lanes as it follows the Missouri plain.
evidence.quote: the two-lane highway becomes a four-lane divided highway as it approaches Dakota City.

evidence.claim: In Blair, US 75 shares Washington Street with US 30 for half a mile before their routes separate.
evidence.quote: together the two routes run concurrently along Washington Street for one-half mile (800 m)

evidence.claim: After the townsite company dissolved, the settlement became Decatur Village in 1858.
evidence.quote: Following the dissolution of the Decatur Townsite and Ferry Company, the town was renamed Decatur Village in 1858.

evidence.claim: The Nebraska Game and Parks Commission acquired the site in 1963, before undertaking the reconstruction; the park includes a military museum.
evidence.quote: The Nebraska Game and Parks Commission gained title to the site in 1963. During the 1980s and 1990s, it reconstructed the fort. Today, Fort Atkinson is a Nebraska state historical park, which includes a military museum.

flags: Length remains inconsistent: NDOT gives 82 miles, the cached tourism page says 131, and the highway article gives 87.32. Material’s 98-mile tourism figure is not what the saved page says. NDOT supplies the overview definition.

No tribal-authored history is cached. Omitted the current 1868 relocation claim pending a suitable tribal or primary source, although the village article repeats it. Living practices are supported by the cached tourism page, not a current tribal event calendar.
Winnebago is shorter than 90 words to avoid padding the limited supported cultural material.
Fort Atkinson remains a separate excursion as supplied, south of the strip-map endpoint at Blair; NDOT and the highway article extend the route toward Omaha.
Corrected the current draft’s compressed claim that the bluff-top fort was built fifteen years after 1804: the river-bottom camp dates to 1819, the bluff-top post to 1820.
